meta.titre: Practical physics: measuring, reducing errors and handling results

sections.contenu_markdown: In a Yaounde school laboratory, two students time a swinging pendulum and get answers that differ by two seconds. One of them gave up after a single swing; the other timed many swings and repeated the test. Practical physics is about this kind of care: choosing the right instrument, reading it correctly, reducing errors and presenting results in a table or on a graph. The GCE O/L tests it both in Paper 1 questions on apparatus and in the practical-style questions of Paper 2.

items: Volume of an irregular solid can be found by displacement of water, in $\mathrm{cm^3}$.
A graph has an independent variable on the horizontal axis and a dependent variable on the vertical axis.
A ticker timer of frequency $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ prints $50$ dots every second.

sections.titre: Doing a reliable practical: instruments, errors and graphs
sections.contenu_markdown:
A good practical answer has four parts: the right **apparatus**, a clear **procedure**, correct **processing of results** and sensible **precautions**.

| Instrument | Measures | Good practice |
|---|---|---|
| Metre rule | length | eye directly above the mark, read from a sharp edge |
| Measuring cylinder | volume of liquid | read at the bottom of the meniscus with eye at the same level |
| Stopwatch | time | time many repeats (for example 20 swings) and divide |
| Thermometer | temperature | keep the bulb in the liquid, stir, wait for a steady value |
| Ammeter and voltmeter | current and voltage | check the zero first; ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel |

**Errors.** A *random error* varies from reading to reading (for example reaction time). It is reduced by taking several readings and finding the **mean**. A *systematic error* shifts every reading the same way (for example a zero error, or a wrongly set instrument). It is removed by correcting the readings or the instrument. **Parallax error** comes from reading a scale with the eye not directly in line.

**Results.** Record readings in a table with headings and units. Plot a graph with the independent variable on the horizontal axis, labelled axes with units, a scale using more than half of the grid, points marked clearly and a *best-fit line* (a smooth line with points on both sides). The **gradient** is $\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ taken from a large triangle drawn on the line, not from two data points.

**Lagging** reduces heat loss to the surroundings in heating experiments. Repeating a measurement and averaging improves reliability.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for a graph, a gradient or a value read from a line.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Choose a scale that is simple (1, 2 or 5 units per large square) and that fills more than half of each axis. Draw the best-fit line, then pick two points far apart **on the line**. The gradient is $\dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$. Read the unit of the gradient from the axes: for extension in cm against load in N, it is cm per N. A line through the origin shows that the two quantities are directly proportional.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a trolley pulls a tape through a timer and the tape is analysed.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ timer gives one dot every $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$, so $10$ dot-spaces last $0.2\ \mathrm{s}$. Speed of a section $=$ length of the section $\div$ its time. If later sections have longer lengths for the same number of spaces, the trolley is speeding up. Acceleration $=$ change in speed $\div$ time between the middles of the two sections.

sections.enonce_markdown: A student finds the density of a small stone. The mass of the stone, measured on a balance, is $31.2\ \mathrm{g}$. A measuring cylinder holds water at the $40.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ mark; after the stone is lowered gently into it on a thread, the water level reads $52.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. Calculate the density of the stone in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and give two precautions.

etapes.action: Find the volume of the stone.
etapes.justification: The rise in water level equals the volume of water displaced, which is the volume of the stone.
Density is mass per unit volume.
Use mass in grams and volume in $\mathrm{cm^3}$ to get $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.
They reduce the main sources of error in this method.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Read the water level at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye at the level of the surface to avoid parallax. Lower the stone slowly on a thread so that no water splashes out and no air bubble sticks to it.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The density of the stone is **2.6 g/cm3**, which is **2 600 kg/m3**.

items.erreur_markdown: A student times one oscillation of a pendulum with a stopwatch and uses that as the period.
items.pourquoi_faux: Reaction time (about 0.2 s) is a large fraction of one short oscillation, so the percentage error is big.
items.correction_markdown: Time 20 or 30 oscillations, divide by the number of oscillations, and repeat to get a mean.

items.erreur_markdown: An ammeter reads 0.1 A before the circuit is switched on, but the student ignores this and records the readings as they are.
items.pourquoi_faux: This is a zero error, a systematic error. Every reading is too high by the same amount.
items.correction_markdown: Note the zero error and subtract it from every reading (or adjust the zero screw before starting).

items.erreur_markdown: A student reads a measuring cylinder by looking down at the top of the water from above.
items.pourquoi_faux: The line of sight is not level with the meniscus, which produces a parallax error.
items.correction_markdown: Put the eye level with the bottom of the curved surface (meniscus) and read there.

items.erreur_markdown: The gradient of a straight-line graph is calculated from two neighbouring data points chosen on the table.
items.pourquoi_faux: Points close together give a large percentage error, and data points may lie off the best-fit line.
items.correction_markdown: Draw a large triangle on the best-fit line, using two points on the line far apart, and read $\Delta y$ and $\Delta x$.

items.enonce_markdown: A student times $30$ complete oscillations of a simple pendulum and records $54.0\ \mathrm{s}$. (a) Calculate the period and the frequency of the pendulum. (b) Reaction-time error in starting and stopping the watch is about $0.2\ \mathrm{s}$. Compare the percentage error if the student had timed only one oscillation with the error when timing $30$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $T = \dfrac{54.0}{30} = 1.80\ \mathrm{s}$ and $f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{1.80} = 0.56\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **Period = 1.80 s, frequency = 0.56 Hz.**

(b) For one oscillation: $\dfrac{0.2}{1.8} \times 100 = 11\%$. For $30$ oscillations: $\dfrac{0.2}{54.0} \times 100 = 0.37\%$. **About 11 % compared with about 0.37 %**, so timing many oscillations greatly reduces the percentage error.

items.enonce_markdown: A $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ ticker timer records the motion of a trolley. In one section of the tape, $10$ dot-spaces measure $8.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. In the next section, also $10$ dot-spaces, the length is $16.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. Calculate (a) the time for $10$ spaces, (b) the speed in each section and (c) the acceleration of the trolley.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Time between dots $= \dfrac{1}{50} = 0.02\ \mathrm{s}$, so $10$ spaces take $10 \times 0.02 = 0.2\ \mathrm{s}$.

(b) First section: $v_1 = \dfrac{0.080}{0.2} = 0.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Second section: $v_2 = \dfrac{0.160}{0.2} = 0.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (lengths converted to metres).

(c) The middles of two consecutive sections are $10$ spaces, that is $0.2\ \mathrm{s}$, apart: $a = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{t} = \dfrac{0.8 - 0.4}{0.2} = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

**Speeds 0.4 m/s and 0.8 m/s; acceleration 2.0 m/s squared.**

items.enonce_markdown: A student measures the resistance of a lamp. The voltmeter reads $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and the ammeter reads $0.60\ \mathrm{A}$. Before the circuit was switched on, the ammeter pointer was at $0.10\ \mathrm{A}$ instead of zero. (a) What kind of error is this? (b) Calculate the resistance with and without correcting for it. (c) Give one precaution that would remove this error.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) It is a **systematic (zero) error**: every ammeter reading is $0.10\ \mathrm{A}$ too high.

(b) Corrected current $= 0.60 - 0.10 = 0.50\ \mathrm{A}$, so $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{3.0}{0.50} = 6.0\ \Omega$. Uncorrected: $R = \dfrac{3.0}{0.60} = 5.0\ \Omega$, which is wrong by $1.0\ \Omega$.

(c) Check the meter reading with the circuit off and adjust the zero screw (or subtract the zero error from every reading).

**Correct resistance = 6.0 ohms (not 5.0 ohms).**

items_markdown: Choose the right instrument and read it correctly: eye level with the scale, bottom of the meniscus, zero checked before use.
Random errors are reduced by repeating readings and taking the mean; systematic errors (such as a zero error) must be corrected.
Time many oscillations and divide: this reduces the percentage error caused by reaction time.
Present results in a table with units and plot a graph with labelled axes, a good scale and a best-fit line; the gradient is $\Delta y / \Delta x$ from a large triangle.
A $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ ticker timer prints a dot every $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$; section speed is length divided by time.
